**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800 (0760), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections (Section A: 1800 - 1922; Section B: 1922 - 1961; Section C: 1961 to present). All the questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 4 » par section (A : questions 1 à 4, B : 5 à 8, C : 9 à 12), c'est-à-dire le minimum imposé ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : « All the questions carry equal marks » et chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter). Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et texte en transparence du verso (illisible, sans rapport) ignorés ; aucune question coupée, aucune carte ni figure.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les dates et noms sont donnés de mémoire historique et sont à faire relire par un historien du Cameroun avant mise en ligne.

Les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `foumban conference of 1961`, `cameroon foreign policy under biya`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à recontrôler à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

Question 11 : le référendum du 20 mai 1972 (résultat présenté comme une très large majorité, sans pourcentage), la Constitution du 2 juin 1972, les sept provinces initiales, le changement de nom de 1984, les Conférences anglophones de Buea (1993) et de Bamenda (1994) et la crise anglophone depuis 2016 sont cités de mémoire ; la présentation des raisons réelles (centralisation du pouvoir) reflète l'interprétation dominante des historiens, nuancée par les raisons officielles.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why and with what consequences was the unitary state created in Cameroon in 1972?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** On 20 May 1972, following a speech by President Ahmadou Ahidjo, the people of Cameroon voted in a referendum, by an overwhelming official majority, to replace the federal system of 1961 by a unitary state. The new constitution of 2 June 1972 created the United Republic of Cameroon. The reasons given by the government were national unity and development, but the move also served political purposes. Its consequences were deep and are still a source of controversy.

**1. Why the unitary state was created**
- *Official reasons.* Ahidjo argued that the federation had been a transitional arrangement and that it was time to build a single, united nation. The existence of two federated states with two governments, assemblies and administrations was said to be costly and to duplicate effort, to slow economic and social development and to keep alive the difference between East and West Cameroon inherited from colonial rule. A single state would, he claimed, strengthen national unity, simplify administration and speed up development.
- *Political reasons: consolidating power.* Ahidjo had always favoured a strong central government. After the creation of the single party, the Cameroon National Union (CNU), in 1966, and the defeat of the UPC rebellion, the federal structure was the last obstacle to full centralisation. The federal system of 1961 had been dominated by the federal President, and the abolition of the autonomy of West Cameroon allowed him to control all the country's institutions and the appointment of officials directly.
- *Weakness of West Cameroon.* By 1972 the Anglophone leaders were divided or integrated into the CNU, and the Prime Minister of West Cameroon, S. T. Muna, supported Ahidjo. There was little organised opposition, and the political conditions were favourable.
- *Economic considerations.* Federal financial control over resources, and the hope of managing the economic potential of West Cameroon (its plantations, ports and the possibility of oil, which was to be exploited from the late 1970s), made a single administration attractive. A unified state would also allow a single national plan.
- *Pressure for assimilation.* A strong Francophone majority and administrative elite favoured a single system, and many people saw federalism as an obstacle to a Cameroonian nation.

**2. Consequences**
- *Political centralisation.* West Cameroon's institutions (the House of Assembly, the House of Chiefs and the position of Prime Minister) were abolished. The country was divided into provinces (seven at first) under appointed governors and prefects, and the powers of the President were greatly increased. This strengthened the one-party state and the personal power of Ahidjo and, later, of his successor.
- *Marginalisation of the Anglophones.* The English-speaking minority lost their autonomy and many felt "assimilated" into a French-dominated system. Anglophones were under-represented in senior posts, and some features of the English-language legal and educational heritage were under pressure. This led to the growth of the "Anglophone problem". In 1984 the name of the state was changed to the Republic of Cameroon, which was interpreted as the denial of the union of two equal partners.
- *National integration and uniform administration.* The unitary system allowed the creation of one national administration, one budget, one development plan and a single system of public services, and it supported the policy of official bilingualism. Supporters regard it as an essential step towards national unity.
- *Long-term effects.* The abolition of federalism produced frustration among Anglophones and later movements such as the Southern Cameroons National Council (1990s), the All Anglophone Conferences of Buea (1993) and Bamenda (1994), and demands for a return to federalism or for secession, leading to the Anglophone crisis from 2016, with violence in the North-West and South-West regions.
- *Economic consequences.* Central control over resources and planning was strengthened, but regional inequalities and marginalisation of some areas persisted.

**Conclusion.** The unitary state of 1972 was created officially to promote national unity and development and to save costs, but also, and mainly, because Ahidjo wished to centralise power at a time when he faced little opposition. Its consequences included stronger presidential power and a more uniform administration, but also the end of the autonomy of West Cameroon, a feeling of marginalisation among Anglophones and the long-term problem which has troubled national unity since the 1990s.
